proposition: For every integer n with 1 <= n <= 60, the sum of k^2 for k = 1..n equals n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 + floor(n/4).
hypotheses: the sum is empty for n = 0

argument.text: The identity holds at n = 1: the left side is 1 and the right side evaluates to 1.
Write F(n) = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 + floor(n/4). For every n with 1 <= n <= 59, F(n+1) - F(n) = (n+1)^2, which is exactly the term added when the upper limit increases by one.
Every integer n in [1, 60] is even or odd, so the two cases below are exhaustive.
For every integer n with 1 <= n <= 60: if n is divisible by 4 then n(n+1)/2 is even.
Put H(n) = n^2 + [n = 3]. Then (n-3)n^2 = (n-3)H(n) for every n in [1, 60].
For every integer n with 2 <= n <= 60 we have n^2 >= 2n.
There exists an integer n in [1, 60] with n^2 > 60.
Base case and increment together establish the identity for every n in [1, 60].
